title: Paddy's Pub: Home of the Original Kitten Mittens

jokes.text: Charlie Kelly introduces himself as 'local business owner and cat enthusiast' in a homemade infomercial
jokes.setup: Cold open plays like a legitimate infomercial with professional framing
jokes.punchline: 'Local business owner AND cat enthusiast' — Charlie's self-identification as a cat enthusiast as a credential is immediately funny, plus the bar owner calling himself a 'local business owner' in a cheesy infomercial tone
jokes.explanation: Perfect character integration — Charlie's earnest self-branding as a 'cat enthusiast' as though it's a professional credential is entirely consistent with his character. The infomercial format parody works because Charlie absolutely would do this. Strong opening.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Hello. Charlie Kelly here, local business owner and cat enthusiast.

jokes.text: Sound effects of ROARING and GLASS SHATTERING playing over footage of a cat, then 'Is your cat clawing at your furnitures?'
jokes.setup: Infomercial problem-solution format; dramatic sound effects imply a monster
jokes.punchline: The catastrophic sound effects (roaring, glass shattering) are for a housecat; compounded by 'furnitures' — a classic Charlie malapropism
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke that earns its high score: the absurd mismatch between monster-movie sound design and a mundane housecat is visually hilarious; then 'furnitures' (the plural) is a perfect Charlie malapropism that couldn't come from any other character. The layering of physical absurdity and linguistic character work is genuinely strong writing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Is your cat constantly stomping around, driving you crazy?

jokes.text: 'You're so stupid! There is.' — Charlie breaks infomercial format to insult the viewer
jokes.setup: Standard infomercial rhetorical beat: 'Think there's no solution?' expects 'Well, think again!'
jokes.punchline: Instead of a friendly redirect, Charlie personally insults the audience — 'You're so stupid!' — before delivering the product name
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and arguably one of the best in the series. The infomercial format sets up an extremely rigid rhetorical expectation, and Charlie's sincere hostility toward the viewer ('You're so stupid!') is a perfect subversion. It's funny on multiple levels: it reveals that Charlie doesn't understand the form he's imitating, it's pure character (Charlie's casual contempt), and it's maximally economical — four words do enormous comedic work. Genuinely exceptional. Comparable to the 8+ anchor examples in wit and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Is your cat clawing at your furnitures? Think there's no answer? You're so stupid!

jokes.text: Cricket sounds after the reveal of Kitten Mittens — a silent reaction beat implying the mittens look terrible on the cat
jokes.setup: Charlie announces 'Kitten Mittens' with great fanfare as an elegant solution.
jokes.punchline: Dead silence (crickets chirping) — the mittens are presumably ridiculous-looking, and the cat immediately yowls in protest.
jokes.explanation: The cricket beat is a classic comedy punctuation mark, but it's well-deployed here because it's followed immediately by the cat's yowl of protest. The double-beat (silence, then screaming cat) is structurally sound. Not original in concept but executes the gag with good timing.

jokes.text: Cat yowls in pain after mittens are applied; Charlie: 'I couldn't hear anything.'
jokes.setup: The whole product premise is that mittens will silence cats
jokes.punchline: The demonstration cat screams in agony from the mittens; Charlie declares success ('I couldn't hear anything') — either oblivious or lying
jokes.explanation: Layered and efficient. The cat's yowl proves the product actively harms the animal while also not solving the noise problem, and Charlie's straight-faced 'I couldn't hear anything' captures his complete disconnect from reality. The ambiguity between obliviousness and shameless lying is very Charlie. High economy — the joke lands in five words.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I couldn't hear anything.

jokes.text: 'Is your cat one-legged? Is your cat fat, skinny or an in-between? That doesn't matter, 'cause one size fits all.'
jokes.setup: Infomercial inclusivity pitch ('works for everyone!')
jokes.punchline: 'One-legged' as the first demographic called out — the most absurdly specific edge case imaginable — before the reassurance that one size fits all (which raises more questions about one-legged cats)
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'one-legged' is delightful — it's the kind of detail only Charlie would think to include, and it raises the implicit question of how one mitten works on a one-legged cat. 'One size fits all' as the resolution compounds the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Is your cat one-legged? Is your cat fat, skinny or an in-between?

jokes.text: 'Kitten Mittens. You'll be smitten.' — Charlie's infomercial tagline with rhyme
jokes.setup: Product pitch reaching its tagline moment
jokes.punchline: Charlie lands on 'You'll be smitten' as his rhyming tagline — it's genuinely a decent rhyme, which is funny because Charlie accidentally wrote something competent
jokes.explanation: A legitimately clever pun that Charlie stumbles into — the irony of Charlie, who mangles language constantly, accidentally producing a good tagline makes it funnier than the pun itself.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Kitten Mittens. You'll be smitten. Mee-ow!

jokes.text: Charlie closes infomercial with 'Mee-ow!' and a button click
jokes.setup: Infomercial is wrapping up with standard sign-off
jokes.punchline: Charlie's earnest cat noise as a professional closing — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfect capper for the infomercial segment. Charlie signing off with a cat meow as though it's standard professional conduct is a small but very Charlie beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Kitten Mittens. You'll be smitten.

jokes.text: Charlie explains Kitten Mittens was inspired by 'a hundred alley cats tapping on my windows, trying to get in' at night
jokes.setup: Gang asks where the Kitten Mittens idea came from
jokes.punchline: Charlie describes a legitimately horrifying scenario (a hundred cats massing at his windows) as a mundane nightly occurrence that simply required a product solution
jokes.explanation: Implies Charlie's life is so chaotic that a nightly siege by a hundred feral cats is simply a problem to be solved rather than an emergency. Pure character-world-building comedy — expands the horror of Charlie's apartment life.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I've been forced to fall asleep to the deafening sound of, like, a hundred alley cats tapping on my windows, trying to get in.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'What do moronic Kitten Mittens have to do with our bar?' / Charlie: 'One, they're not moronic, they're awesome. And two, uh, nothing.'
jokes.setup: Dennis raises the obvious objection — why is a cat mitten product relevant to the bar?
jokes.punchline: Charlie structures his defense formally ('One... and two...') but his second point is simply a full admission that it has nothing to do with the bar
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — the 'One... Two...' format creates the expectation of a rationalization, and the blunt admission on point two is a perfect subversion. Charlie's simultaneous defensiveness about his product AND total honesty about its irrelevance is great character work. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What do moronic Kitten Mittens have to do with our bar?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Okay. One, they're not moronic. They're awesome.

jokes.text: Mac enthusiastically pitches T-shirts, beach towels, and 'those nudie pens' as merchandise
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to show enthusiasm for the merchandising idea
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from normal (T-shirts) to slightly odd (beach towels) to 'nudie pens' — cheap novelty pens with naked ladies, which Mac mentions with equal enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Classic rule-of-three with an absurd third item. 'Nudie pens' feels authentic to what Mac would pitch and to the bar's brand. Solid mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We could do T-shirts. We could do beach towels, those nudie pens.

jokes.text: Dee reveals she owns 100% of the bar's merchandising rights; Dennis and Mac laugh, then are horrified when she produces the contract
jokes.setup: Dee claims a contract gives her all merchandising rights; Dennis and Mac dismiss it
jokes.punchline: She actually has the contract — the boys signed it to underpay her and it backfired spectacularly
jokes.explanation: Good structural irony — the boys' own scheme to exploit Dee created the instrument of their defeat. Classic IASIP karma-free irony where their schemes undo them.

dialogue.line: We got you to sign that contract so we could pay you less than minimum wage.

jokes.text: Mac eats the contract while Dennis and Charlie distract Dee
jokes.setup: Dee is about to prove her legal rights with the physical contract
jokes.punchline: Mac simply eats the document — a physically absurd, childish solution executed with apparent seriousness
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny physical escalation — the gang's response to a legal document is to destroy the evidence by eating it. The casualness with which this is executed as an obvious solution is very IASIP. Sets up the later callback beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh! You son of a bitch! That doesn't nullify it, you know?

jokes.text: Dee: 'You can't just go eat a contract!' / Charlie: 'He just did eat it.'
jokes.setup: Dee protests the eating of the contract as legally invalid
jokes.punchline: Charlie's matter-of-fact correction — 'He just did eat it' — treats the eating as a factual observation rather than engaging with her legal point
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical. Charlie correcting the impossible with the actual — a perfect deadpan response that sidesteps the entire legal argument with a tautology. 'He just did eat it' is a very quotable line.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I don't, but you can't just go eat a contract!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He just did eat it.

jokes.text: Charlie accuses Dennis of secretly wanting to steal Kitten Mittens, saying 'I can see it in your eyes'
jokes.setup: Charlie is paranoid about intellectual property theft
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects him — he doesn't want Kitten Mittens, he wants the merchandising concept — but then immediately reveals his instinct to steal the idea IS very strong (just the right idea)
jokes.explanation: Good beat — Charlie's paranoia is validated but misdirected. Dennis's clarification ('not Kitten Mittens, idiot, the merchandising concept') is a nice character distinction.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You don't have a leg to stand on.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I gotta say, Mac, my instinct to steal this idea is very strong.' / Mac: 'Kitten Mittens?' / Dennis: 'No, idiot. Merchandising in the bar.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac are discussing Charlie's pitch
jokes.punchline: Dennis's casual admission that his first instinct is theft, followed by needing to correct Mac's assumption
jokes.explanation: Dennis's unembarrassed admission that his reflex is theft is perfect character work. Efficient and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Kitten Mittens? No, idiot. Merchandising in the bar.

jokes.text: Frank pitches hard-boiled Paddy's-branded eggs to keep on your desk or car dashboard
jokes.setup: Gang is brainstorming legitimate merchandise
jokes.punchline: Frank's contribution is branded hard-boiled eggs — a perishable food item with no obvious merchandising logic — and his 'dashboard of your car' escalation makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Deeply Frank-specific — his obsession with eggs is a running character trait, and the specificity of the dashboard location ('not just your desk — also your car!') as a selling point is perfect absurdist escalation. High character integration because only Frank Reynolds would pitch branded eggs as premium merchandise.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I've never been to Fiji.

jokes.text: 'Keeping hard-boiled eggs on your desktop or the dashboard of your car is not a jumping-off point. Get the hell out of here.'
jokes.setup: Frank insists his egg idea is 'a jumping-off point'
jokes.punchline: The gang's rejection is a straight-faced statement that an egg on your dashboard is not, in fact, a jumping-off point
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction to Frank's absurdity. The specific call-out of 'dashboard of your car' makes it more than a generic dismissal, but it's a supporting joke rather than a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: How about, like, hard-boiled eggs from Paddy's Bar? Green eggs. Says 'Paddy's' on them. You keep them on your desk when you go to work.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie's plan to get on the lawyer's good side: compliment his wife's good looks
jokes.setup: Mac acknowledges the lawyer doesn't like them and they need to charm him
jokes.punchline: His charm strategy is to compliment the wife's photo — but as we're immediately told, the wife looks like 'a stone-cold bitch'
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the upcoming lawyer scene. The gap between Mac's diplomatic instinct and the actual reality of the wife's appearance is established before we see the payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Then you put it on your dashboard of your car.

jokes.text: Mac: 'That woman looks like a stone-cold bitch, and you know it. And he knows it 'cause he turns the picture away from him.'
jokes.setup: Mac was suggesting complimenting the lawyer's wife as a charm tactic
jokes.punchline: Mac's brutal assessment of the wife's appearance, followed by his amateur detective logic about the turned-away photo
jokes.explanation: The pivot from charm strategy to brutal honesty is funny, and 'stone-cold bitch' is a great line. The 'turned-away photo' logic establishes a mystery that pays off perfectly later when the real explanation is revealed. Good structural setup.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't get it?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You don't get it!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't get it?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You don't get it!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah? We'll see who doesn't get it!

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I was not participating in that conversation, 'cause I don't find her lovely. I think you can do better than that. And I mean that as a compliment.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are awkwardly insisting the wife is lovely to the lawyer
jokes.punchline: Charlie dissociates from the lie, then tells the lawyer he can do better than his wife — presenting this devastating insult as a compliment
jokes.explanation: Layered and excellent. Charlie refuses to participate in the lie (honest), then immediately insults the wife worse than Mac did (terrible), and frames the insult as a sincere compliment (delusional). 'And I mean that as a compliment' is a perfectly Charlie non-sequitur tag. This is strong joke construction.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That woman looks like a stone-cold bitch, and you know it. And he knows it 'cause he turns the picture away from him.

jokes.text: Mac: 'We're both men of the law... we jabber-jaw, we go tit for tat...' / Lawyer: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to establish a rapport with the lawyer using legal-sounding camaraderie
jokes.punchline: The lawyer responds to Mac's entire elaborate speech about mutual respect with a single 'No.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. Mac's speech builds and builds with quasi-legal nonsense ('jabber-jaw', 'tit for tat', 'mutual respect') and the lawyer's monosyllabic 'No.' destroys it completely. Maximum economy on the punchline. Classic straight-man/fool structure executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I was not participating in that conversation, 'cause I don't find her lovely. I think you're better than that. I think you can do better than that. And I mean that as a compliment.

jokes.text: Lawyer: 'Any respect that you're feeling that's coming from me is a mistake on your part.' / Charlie: 'Then I'll just regress, 'cause I feel like I've made myself perfectly redundant.'
jokes.setup: Lawyer corrects Mac's delusion about mutual respect
jokes.punchline: Charlie responds with 'I'll just regress' (meaning 'digress') and 'made myself perfectly redundant' (meaning 'clear') — malapropisms that form an accidentally coherent but wrong sentence
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. 'Perfectly redundant' instead of 'perfectly clear' is a beautiful malapropism because it's also accidentally true — Charlie HAS made himself redundant. The lawyer's confirming 'Yes, you have' adds a perfect button. High originality because the wordplay works on two levels simultaneously. This is very strong character-specific writing — only Charlie Kelly would use 'redundant' here.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: I do charge. Okay? You don't pay.

jokes.text: Charlie asks lawyer if a contract holds up 'if it has been ingested by the other party'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to frame legal questions in formal-sounding language
jokes.punchline: 'Ingested' as a legal term for 'Mac ate it' — Charlie's attempt at legal vocabulary applied to a ridiculous physical act
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the word 'ingested' is doing the work, translating Mac's animal behavior into legalese. Charlie's attempts at formal register always produce comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We're both men of the law. You know? We get after it. You know? We jabber-jaw. We go tit for tat.

jokes.text: Charlie casually adds 'I'm also gonna need a patent for the Kitten Mittens' mid-legal-consultation
jokes.setup: Serious legal meeting about contract law
jokes.punchline: Charlie treats his cat mittens patent as an equally urgent legal matter requiring the same meeting
jokes.explanation: Functional beat — Charlie's total equivalence between serious legal matters and Kitten Mittens is consistent character work, though not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Then I'll just regress, 'cause I feel like I've made myself perfectly redundant.

jokes.text: Lawyer's secretary bursts in: 'I'm sorry, sir. But they locked me in a closet.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are conducting their legal meeting
jokes.punchline: The reveal that they locked the lawyer's secretary in a closet to gain access — a detail mentioned as though it's incidental
jokes.explanation: Great reveal. The casualness with which the secretary mentions being locked in a closet, as though this is simply an inconvenience rather than a crime, is perfect for the show's tone. The delay makes it funnier — we didn't know the full extent of Mac and Charlie's entry plan.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: the heretofore document had- had dry ink on it for at least many 'forknights,'

jokes.text: Mac reveals the Paddy's Pub thong while wearing it — 'You're wearing women's underwear?' / 'Yeah, bro!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are pitching merchandise ideas
jokes.punchline: Mac's pitch involves him personally modeling women's thong underwear — apparently he put it on for the presentation
jokes.explanation: Good visual reveal — Mac's enthusiasm for wearing the thong himself, with no apparent self-consciousness, plays into his homoeroticism-he-doesn't-acknowledge character thread. 'Yeah, bro!' as a proud confirmation is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Secretary
dialogue.line: But they locked me in a closet.

jokes.text: Dennis's towel pitch: big illustrated dick on the front, then he whips the towel away to reveal a tiny baby dick
jokes.setup: Dennis explains the comedy concept: guy comes out of shower with a comically large illustrated penis on the towel
jokes.punchline: The towel drops to reveal a tiny illustrated penis — the whole thing is an elaborate visual bait-and-switch
jokes.explanation: Classic dick joke with a decent two-stage structure. The 'that's not how you see yourself though?' line from Mac adds a character wrinkle. Dicktowel.com is the stronger element of this bit (see next joke).

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Let me show you mine, then you can go first. Then I'd be going second.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Already did it.' / Mac: 'You did?' / Dennis: 'Dicktowel.com.'
jokes.setup: Mac suggests they set up a website
jokes.punchline: Dennis has already registered Dicktowel.com — the efficiency and confidence of this commitment to a crude joke
jokes.explanation: Perfect punchline economy. The website already being registered (and actually being dicktowel.com in real life — which the writers set up) is a great commitment gag. 'Dicktowel.com' as a standalone line is extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Paddy's thong, dude! Paddy's thong!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're wearing women's underwear?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, bro! You bet your ass I'm wearing women's underwear.

jokes.text: Frank bursts in: 'Well, you don't think I know what's going on? Huh? Open your mouth, bitch!' then blasts tequila into 'Brenda's' face
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis's calm pitch session
jokes.punchline: Frank explodes into the room, aggressively guns tequila at a woman's face, and declares this his merchandising idea
jokes.explanation: Great Frank entrance — the aggression, the screaming, the random woman being shot with tequila as a demonstration. Very high character integration because only Frank would think violence is a selling point. 'Open your mouth, bitch!' as the sales pitch line is darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What's more sexual than a high-waisted thong riding high up a woman's backside? Nothing.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I haven't figured out how to get the tequila to come out of the barrel of the gun. But I'm working on it.'
jokes.setup: Dee is upset that Frank shot tequila in her eye
jokes.punchline: Frank acknowledges the gun doesn't work as intended but presents this as a minor engineering problem rather than a reason to abandon the concept
jokes.explanation: Frank's calm acknowledgment that he's already shooting people with a malfunctioning tequila gun and plans to continue until he gets it right is a great deadpan. The confidence in a terrible product under development is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm wearing them because I want to turn you on.

jokes.text: Mac to Frank: 'So this is your plan? You're gonna go into the convention waving a gun in people's faces, throwing tequila in everybody's eyes, with a big-titted woman?' / Frank: 'Duh, yeah!'
jokes.setup: Mac is summarizing Frank's business plan skeptically
jokes.punchline: 'Duh, yeah!' — Frank's summary was accurate and he's confused why it's being questioned
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP straight-man-realizes-there-is-no-straight-man structure. Mac's incredulous summary is accurate; Frank's 'Duh, yeah!' confirms it without irony. Great character work.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You drew a men's buttocks on a towel.

jokes.text: Frank reveals his final idea: a Paddy's Pub stress ball — which is just an egg
jokes.setup: Frank is pitching merchandise ideas; he's been told to get out for the egg idea
jokes.punchline: The 'stress ball' is the same hard-boiled egg he was pitching before, now rebranded
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback structure — Frank's egg idea was rejected, so he rebranded it as a stress ball. Dennis's 'Oh, goddamn it, Frank! That's just an egg!' followed by Frank's 'It's a jumping-off point. Get out!' is a beautiful circular callback that escalates the original joke. Frank's refusal to change the actual product, just the marketing, is very character-specific and matches the show's theme of branding as delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, it's a baby dick.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah! We're gonna sell a million of these, dude.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie staking out the lawyer at a 'shady motel' because they think he's having an affair they can blackmail him with
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie need the lawyer's services
jokes.punchline: Their plan is not to pay him legitimately but to blackmail him into working for free — and they've been surveilling a motel all night for evidence
jokes.explanation: Good establishment of the gang's moral framework — blackmail is their first instinct. The motel stakeout is funny as a premise.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We'll do black ones and yellow ones for the Asians.

jokes.text: Mac insisting the lawyer's wife is not attractive while the lawyer's photo turns away from him — Charlie sees this as proof of shame
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are building their blackmail theory
jokes.punchline: Their amateur detective logic (turned photo = guilt, motel = affair) will be systematically dismantled by the real explanation
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the divorce reveal payoff. Works as misdirection — the audience is building toward one conclusion (affair) that gets subverted.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, it's a baby dick.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We're gonna sell a million of these, dude.

jokes.text: Charlie spots a woman in the motel eating an entire sleeve of Chips Ahoy and gets distracted; Mac has to tell him 'we're not here to blackmail a lady for eating too many cookies'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are conducting a surveillance stakeout
jokes.punchline: Charlie's attention drifts to an unrelated woman, and Mac has to explicitly clarify that cookie-eating is not blackmail-worthy
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'We're not here to blackmail a lady for eating too many cookies' is an extraordinary line because (a) it implies Charlie WAS considering this, (b) it requires Mac to state something that should never need to be said, and (c) it characterizes both men perfectly — Charlie's chaotic focus and Mac's relative but still absurd reasonableness. Highly quotable, completely original, great economy. This is the 8+ anchor-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Open your mouth, bitch. Prepare to be blasted, bitch!

jokes.text: Mac: 'We're not here to blackmail a lady for eating too many cookies.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is reporting the cookie-eating woman as surveillance news.
jokes.punchline: Mac's reality check — but phrased as 'we're not here to blackmail a lady for eating too many cookies,' which implies that in other circumstances, that WOULD be something they'd consider.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The word 'here' does enormous work — 'we're not here to' implies that blackmailing cookie-eaters is a thing they might do in other contexts, it's just not today's mission. It's a perfect Always Sunny line: Mac is being the relatively reasonable one while revealing how deep the gang's moral baseline is underground. Highly quotable, great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's a gun that shoots liquor into your mouth!

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie are discovered hiding in the lawyer's car. Lawyer: 'All right. Um, so what are you people doing in my car now?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie hid in the lawyer's car overnight after getting cold during the stakeout
jokes.punchline: The lawyer discovers them in his car, apparently not surprised enough to skip 'all right' and 'now' — implying this is not his first experience of IASIP nonsense
jokes.explanation: The lawyer's weary 'now' — as though this is an ongoing pattern — is a good character beat. His resignation to the gang's presence is funnier than shock would be.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You threw tequila in my eye!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, I haven't figured out how to get the tequila to come out of the barrel of the gun.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie explain they 'jimmied the lock and spent the night' in the lawyer's car because the stakeout got cold
jokes.setup: Lawyer asks why they're in his car
jokes.punchline: The practical explanation — it got cold, so they broke into his car to sleep — is delivered as though it's a completely reasonable sequence of events
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the casual explanation of breaking and entering as a weather-related decision is very IASIP. Their total lack of guilt is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Paddy's Pub stress ball. You give this to people. They put it on their desk.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, goddamn it, Frank! That's just an egg!

jokes.text: Mac tells the lawyer directly: 'Because you're having an affair, and we're gonna blackmail you for your services.'
jokes.setup: Lawyer asks why they were spying on him
jokes.punchline: Mac states their blackmail plan with complete straightforwardness — no euphemism, no embarrassment
jokes.explanation: The directness is the joke — no one who was planning blackmail would typically announce it. Mac's total absence of shame is perfect character work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The woman in the room right next to him... she just ate an entire sleeve of Chips Ahoy!

jokes.text: The lawyer reveals his wife is leaving him and he's been crying in a motel — which explains all of Mac and Charlie's 'evidence' of an affair
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie built an entire blackmail theory on a turned photo, motel stay, and apparent crying
jokes.punchline: The real explanation is completely innocent and heartbreaking — the lawyer's wife is leaving him. The detective work was entirely wrong.
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent payoff — every piece of Mac and Charlie's 'evidence' gets explained innocently and painfully. The cringe of watching them realize they broke into a grieving man's car to blackmail him over his wife leaving is a classic IASIP dark comedy beat. High structure score because all the setup elements resolve cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: she just ate an entire sleeve of Chips Ahoy!

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Mmm. Sad.' — responding to the lawyer's divorce revelation
jokes.setup: Lawyer has just shared deeply personal grief about his divorce
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response is an almost performatively minimal acknowledgment — 'Mmm. Sad.' — as though processing it briefly before moving on
jokes.explanation: Two words doing enormous work. 'Mmm. Sad.' captures Charlie's total emotional inadequacy — it's the sort of thing you say when someone's pet dies, not when you've been breaking into their car to exploit their marital pain. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We're not here to blackmail a lady for eating too many cookies.

jokes.text: Charlie immediately pivots from acknowledging the divorce to asking if the lawyer will still help with their Kitten Mitten patent
jokes.setup: Lawyer has just revealed devastating personal news
jokes.punchline: Charlie asks 'So, um — do you want to have a conversation about helping us out with our Kitten Mitten patent?' within seconds of the revelation
jokes.explanation: Cringe-perfect — Charlie's total inability to maintain even a moment of human decency before returning to his agenda. The Kitten Mittens as an equal-weight concern to a man's marital collapse is the irony.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We were staking you out last night- kinda spying on you. It got a little cold. It dropped down, right? So we jimmied your lock and spent the night in here.

jokes.text: Mac demonstrating Paddy's Shotgun to convention-goers: blasting water in someone's face and complaining the technology 'just isn't there'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are testing their shotgun product
jokes.punchline: The gun shoots water (not alcohol) poorly; Mac's response is to blame the technology rather than the concept
jokes.explanation: Continuation of the shotgun gag — the product still doesn't work. The 'technology just isn't there' line is good, implying they've thought carefully about this problem.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Because you're having an affair, and we're gonna blackmail you for your services.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'They did sort of figure it out with water guns, so I don't know why...' / Mac: 'Yeah, but a water gun doesn't have the same feel to it. You want to taste the metal. You want to feel the steel, man.'
jokes.setup: Dennis notes water guns already exist and work
jokes.punchline: Mac insists the product requires a real gun because you need to 'taste the metal' — revealing the core appeal is the gun experience, not the alcohol delivery
jokes.explanation: Mac's revelation of the true appeal — 'you want to taste the metal' — is funny because it accidentally reveals a disturbing product desire that has nothing to do with drinking alcohol. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: my wife is leaving me. And I have to sleep in this fleabag motel.

jokes.text: Dennis's convention video concept: eagles flying through the air, picking up trout from rivers, 'ripping it apart and eating it'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are describing what their promotional video needs to feel like
jokes.punchline: Dennis's vision of 'cool' is nature documentary predator footage — specific, oddly violent, and completely disconnected from alcohol
jokes.explanation: Dennis's specific vision of 'cool' — eagles violently eating trout — is very character-specific to his grandiose self-image. Good absurdist beat.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: my wife is leaving me. And I have to sleep in this fleabag motel.

jokes.text: Frank returns with 'Paddy's Shotgun, bro!' — a modified bigger gun — having clearly stolen Mac and Dennis's idea
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis stole Frank's tequila gun concept and renamed it 'Paddy's Shotgun'
jokes.punchline: Frank returns with an even bigger gun, stealing the concept back — escalating the arms race of idea theft
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the idea-theft theme that runs through the episode. Frank's physical return with an even bigger gun is a classic IASIP escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You just cannot blast water out of a gun. The technology is just not there.

jokes.text: Mac: 'That's the American way, bro. Take a look at Hard Rock Cafe — tweaked by Planet Hollywood. Coke tweaked by Pepsi. Transformers tweaked by GoBots.'
jokes.setup: Frank accuses Mac and Dennis of stealing his gun idea
jokes.punchline: Mac defends idea theft as 'the American way' and cites examples — but his examples are increasingly inapt (GoBots as the Pepsi to Transformers is a great deflating third example)
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The list follows a perfect escalation-deflation pattern: Hard Rock/Planet Hollywood (legitimate), Coke/Pepsi (legitimate), Transformers/GoBots (GoBots is a notoriously inferior knockoff — the exact opposite of Mac's argument). The GoBots example inadvertently proves Frank's point. This is clever writing — Mac's defense of theft accidentally undermines itself. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You want to feel the weight of a real gun in your mouth. You want to taste the metal. You want to feel the steel, man

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie bring a prostitute named Sandy to the lawyer's office as 'compensation' for unpaid legal work
jokes.setup: Lawyer has not been paid; Mac and Charlie feel they owe him
jokes.punchline: Their payment for professional legal services is a prostitute — presented warmly and with apparent sincerity as a fair exchange
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP dark comedy — their version of making good on a debt is hiring a sex worker. The sincerity with which they present this ('she knows all about everything that's going on') compounds the cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: eagles flying through the air and picking up trout out of rivers and shit. Ripping it apart and eating it

jokes.text: Charlie to the lawyer: 'Look at this freakish whore we found.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are presenting Sandy to the lawyer as compensation
jokes.punchline: Charlie's sales pitch for the prostitute is 'freakish whore' — both insulting to Sandy and an odd sales technique
jokes.explanation: Dark humor that's more shock than craft. Charlie's total lack of awareness that this is an insult is character-consistent, but the line itself relies primarily on transgression.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We took what was a good idea and we made it a great idea.

jokes.text: Frank offers the lawyer a 'frame bang' — slipping into his house and 'easing into' his wife so they're both cheating
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to help the lawyer with his divorce
jokes.punchline: Frank's solution to the lawyer's marital problems is to secretly have sex with his wife as a legal strategy — a 'frame bang'
jokes.explanation: One of the best Frank jokes in the episode. 'Frame bang' as a branded term for a specific non-consensual scheme is darkly brilliant — Frank has thought about this enough to give it a name and explain the mechanics. The legal reasoning (mutual infidelity = divorce protection) is twisted but has its own horrible logic. High originality, very Frank-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Take a look at Hard Rock Cafe. Got tweaked by Planet Hollywood. Coke got tweaked by Pepsi. Transformers got tweaked by GoBots.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Bro, rape? I wasn't talking about raping your wife. I was talking about making love to her sweetly while she sleeps.'
jokes.setup: Lawyer objects to Frank's 'frame bang' plan as rape
jokes.punchline: Mac's clarification that 'making love to her sweetly while she sleeps' is not rape — a distinction that is not a distinction
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy — Mac's sincere correction that 'making love sweetly while she sleeps' is different from rape reveals his complete moral blindness. The euphemism 'making love to her sweetly' makes it funnier and more disturbing. Very high quotability — this line is a classic IASIP moment. The structure (objection → clarification that's worse than the original) is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Lawyer, check out this freakish whore we found.

jokes.text: Dee explains her legal grievance: 'This one ate a contract that said I got all the rights to the Paddy's Pub merchandise.'
jokes.setup: Lawyer asks what Dee's suit is about
jokes.punchline: 'This one ate a contract' — delivered with the flat resignation of someone who has accepted this as a normal event
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. 'This one' as the identifier (pointing at Mac) rather than his name implies the kind of exasperated familiarity with his behavior. The deadpan delivery of a genuinely insane legal situation is classic.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I slip into your house one night while your wife is sleeping, and I ease into her real nice.

jokes.text: Lawyer suggests settling for 50%; Dennis whispers to Mac: 'I'll just eat the contract later.'
jokes.setup: Legal settlement is being agreed to
jokes.punchline: Dennis has learned from Mac's earlier move — his plan for dealing with the new contract is to eat it too
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback structure. The episode established contract-eating as Mac's solution; now Dennis casually plans to do the same thing to the resolution contract. It's funny because they've adopted eating contracts as a standing legal strategy. 'I'll just eat the contract later' is a highly quotable line and structurally the callback lands with great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I wasn't talking about raping your wife. I was talking about making love to her sweetly while she sleeps.

jokes.text: Mac shouts 'Objection!' in a non-courtroom legal meeting; the lawyer says 'This is not a court of law'; Mac shouts 'Sustained!'
jokes.setup: The lawyer is trying to mediate a settlement in his office.
jokes.punchline: Mac shouts courtroom objections in what is explicitly not a court. When corrected, he responds with 'Sustained!' — the ruling on his own objection, from the wrong person.
jokes.explanation: Mac shouting 'Sustained!' — the judge's ruling, not a litigant's move — after the lawyer corrects him is a lovely beat. He's not just misusing legal terms, he's responding to a correction with more misused legal terms. Very economical and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: This one ate a contract that said I got all the rights to the Paddy's Pub merchandise.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That never happened.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It happened!

jokes.text: In the middle of the legal settlement, Frank fires his tequila gun at Dee; Frank: 'I made tequila bullets, but I guess I put too much gunpowder in'
jokes.setup: Lawyer is trying to settle multiple disputes simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Frank fires his gun in the room, drenching everyone; his explanation reveals he attempted to make actual explosive projectiles filled with tequila
jokes.explanation: Excellent Frank moment. 'I made tequila bullets, but I guess I put too much gunpowder in' implies (a) Frank has genuine access to gunpowder and ammunition-making equipment, (b) he has been working on this engineering problem seriously, and (c) the solution to 'too much gunpowder' is simply 'less gunpowder' — the concept itself is not the problem. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'll just eat the contract later.

jokes.text: Following the gunshot, everyone immediately pivots to: 'We are taking that propulsion and putting it in our shotgun!' / 'Two guns!' / 'Six boobs!' / 'We're all on the same team!'
jokes.setup: Frank's gun just exploded in the lawyer's office
jokes.punchline: The gang's immediate response to an explosive near-disaster is not concern but enthusiasm for the technology — they're now collaborating
jokes.explanation: 'Six boobs!' as the rallying cry for their new partnership is a great absurdist escalation. The gang's total indifference to the near-explosion and immediate pivot to business is very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: How did you get that much propulsion on the gun?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I made tequila bullets, but I guess I put too much gunpowder in.

jokes.text: 'I made tequila bullets, but I guess I put too much gunpowder in.'
jokes.setup: Frank's gun has just achieved catastrophic propulsion, drenching everyone.
jokes.punchline: Frank's calm, iterative explanation: he made tequila bullets (a phrase that shouldn't exist), and the only issue was calibrating the gunpowder. The 'I guess' acknowledges a small miscalculation.
jokes.explanation: Frank explaining 'tequila bullets' as a legitimate engineering concept is excellent character comedy. The word 'tequila bullets' implies a whole world of Frank's basement experiments. His mild regret ('I guess I put too much gunpowder') is perfect deadpan — no apology, just engineering notes. High character integration: only Frank would have both the resources and the recklessness to make tequila bullets.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Six boobs! We're all on the same team!

jokes.text: Lawyer: 'I will take care of all of your legal needs if each of you agrees to never seek my legal advice again.'
jokes.setup: Chaos has erupted in the lawyer's office
jokes.punchline: The lawyer's deal — do all the work for free in exchange for never seeing them again — is a logical response that reveals how traumatizing the gang is
jokes.explanation: Good payoff for the lawyer's accumulated suffering. The deal — paying in future absence rather than money — captures exactly how terrible the gang is. Classic straight-man-at-the-end-of-his-rope beat.

dialogue.speaker: Secretary
dialogue.line: So sorry, sir. They duct-taped me to the bathroom sink.

jokes.text: The convention video: Frank slurring 'How about a shot?' while visibly drunk, then 'This is how we do it' plays and Mac delivers a deep-voiced 'Paddy's Pub, home of the original shotgun and gun shot!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis's convention pitch video plays
jokes.punchline: The 'cool' video they described (eagles, quick cuts, awesome music) is apparently this — Frank drunk, bad editing, and Mac overdoing the announcer voice
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the elaborate video concept — the gap between their vision and the execution is a classic comedy structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Awesome! I'm wasted!

jokes.text: Convention audience screams in terror as the video ends — presumably from tequila gun demonstration
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis's convention video/presentation is playing
jokes.punchline: The presentation ends with screaming — a terrible result received with 'Huh. That did not look cool.'
jokes.explanation: Good understated reaction. 'Huh. That did not look cool.' as the postmortem is classic Dennis — his aesthetic concern ('it didn't look cool') rather than 'we just terrorized people.'

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: People love stupid shit!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why do you keep calling it stupid though?

jokes.text: Charlie enters victorious: 'Guess who just found some investors for Kitten Mittens!' / Dennis: 'People love stupid shit!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis's elaborate presentation failed; Charlie's infomercial apparently succeeded
jokes.punchline: Charlie's absurd cat mittens found investors; Dennis's summary 'people love stupid shit' is a self-indicting observation — he's just as stupid
jokes.explanation: Good ironic reversal. Dennis dismissing Kitten Mittens as 'stupid shit' while having just presented a tequila gun and dick towels to a screaming audience is nice self-indicting irony.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: The contract that you all blindly signed grants me 100% of the profits from any merchandising opportunities

jokes.text: The lawyer reveals he tricked the entire gang into signing a contract giving him 100% of profits and a restraining order against them
jokes.setup: Gang celebrates their legal victory and Kitten Mittens investment
jokes.punchline: The lawyer out-schemed the gang — he got them to sign away everything AND got a restraining order, all while they thought they were winning
jokes.explanation: Strong structural comedy — the lawyer's revenge is proportionate and clever. The reveal that the settlement Charlie objected to was actually the trap closing on them is good plotting. The restraining order as a bonus is a great escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, that's what the hooker was for!

jokes.text: 'Well, that's what the hooker was for!' — Charlie's response to the lawyer revealing he got paid through the contract
jokes.setup: The lawyer says he 'had to get paid somehow' via the contract.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate counter: they already paid him — with the prostitute they brought. The lawyer's contract scheme was unnecessary; they had already arranged sex-based compensation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback delivery. Charlie's indignant 'That's what the hooker was for!' implies he sees his prostitute-as-payment arrangement as the legitimate and binding form of compensation, and the contract as the redundant scheme. The lawyer's 'Touché. You out-lawyered me there.' is both funny and perfectly in character for someone increasingly broken by this gang.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: the contract that you all signed also included a restraining order? Which you're all currently violating.

jokes.text: Charlie tries to eat the lawyer's contract — but the lawyer reveals he made hundreds of copies
jokes.setup: Charlie spots the contract and lunges for it to eat it; this has worked before
jokes.punchline: The lawyer anticipated the eating strategy and made hundreds of copies — the whole gang's signature move is now useless
jokes.explanation: The best structural joke in the episode. The contract-eating gag was established at 02:50, confirmed as strategy by Dennis at 15:46, and now pays off with the perfect counter-move. 'Fortunately, I made hundreds of copies of that' destroys the gang's entire defensive playbook in one line. The structure is near-perfect — setup, escalation, payoff, counter-payoff all serving the same joke. This is genuinely excellent sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It's still new enough to be edible. That's an edible contract!

jokes.text: Charlie tries to eat the lawyer's contract — but it's new enough to be edible and actually works
jokes.setup: The contract-eating has been established as a viable strategy. The lawyer has just produced his controlling contract.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately eats it. 'It's still new enough to be edible. That's an edible contract! Right in your face!'
jokes.explanation: Triple callback payoff — the contract-eating gag has been building all episode (Dennis ate Dee's contract, Mac planned to eat the settlement contract, now Charlie eats the lawyer's contract). The concept of 'edibility' as a legal criterion — 'it's still new enough to be edible' — is a great escalation of the gag's internal logic. 'Right in your face!' as a victory cry is excellent. The lawyer's response ('I made hundreds of copies of that') is the perfect final deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: You know, fortunately, I made hundreds of copies of that.

jokes.text: Final shot: Charlie is still eating the already-eaten contract in silence; someone off-screen says 'You can probably stop eating that now.'
jokes.setup: Charlie started eating the contract in triumph; the lawyer revealed it's useless
jokes.punchline: Charlie is apparently still eating in the closing beat; the quiet 'you can probably stop eating that now' is the last joke of the episode
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing beat. The whole episode's contract-eating thread ends with Charlie, having lost everything, still mechanically eating a now-pointless piece of paper. The gentle 'you can probably stop eating that now' (not even angry, just tired) is the ideal understated button for the show's tone. Very high economy — the visual plus one line says everything about Charlie's condition. Great callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You can probably stop eating that now.

tmdb_overview: The gang decides to expand their business by developing a number of products that they could sell at Paddy's pub.
